evidence.title: SAME / SAME-R — investigation overview (not test results)
evidence.text: OVERVIEW / OBJECTIVES ONLY. Characterize spacecraft-material smoke and assess smoke-detector response in reduced gravity. Materials: Smoke generated from spacecraft materials; the overview lists Teflon, Kapton, cellulose and silicone rubber. Hardware: Smoke-generation, aerosol measurement and detector-test apparatus; configurations need the original investigation documentation. Measurements: Aerosol number, size and mass-related measurements, plus ionization and photoelectric detector evaluation. NASA reports material-dependent smoke-size distributions; these aggregate results are not individual detector-performance records. Limits: No numerical SAME detector-performance time series are curated here. The NASA document includes aggregate smoke-property results; source-table smoke-generation conditions do not establish alarm sensitivity, false-alarm rate or timing for a chosen habitat. Source: NASA SAME / SAME-R document, PDF pages 1–2 and reflight section.

liveAi.question: Summarize the BASS-II low-airflow findings. Identify limits before applying them to a lunar habitat; do not predict safety.

evidence.title: Reported observation (bass-thickness)
evidence.text: "At the lowest speeds examined (less than 1 cm/s) all the flames tended to become dim blue and very stable. However, heat loss at these very low convective rates is small so the flames can burn for a long time." (source: bass-thickness, PDF page 54) Campaign annotation: this publication concerns original BASS. Do not relabel it as a BASS-II measurement; the two are grouped for discovery only.

evidence.title: Reported observation (bass2-summary)
evidence.text: "Flames survived at airflow less than 1 cm/s." (source: bass2-summary, PDF page 74)

evidence.title: Reported observation (bass-thickness)
evidence.text: "Microgravity flames were found to be especially sensitive to air flow speed in the range 0 to 5 cm/s." evidence.title: BASS / BASS-II — investigation overview (not test results)
evidence.text: OVERVIEW / OBJECTIVES ONLY. Investigate solid-fuel ignition, spread and extinction under controlled low-speed flow. Materials: Plastic films, rods and composite fabric; exact materials and sizes are test-specific. Hardware: BASS-II flow duct in the ISS Microgravity Science Glovebox; video camera with data overlay and a 35-mm still camera. Apparatus details are campaign-specific. Measurements: For BASS-II, CSA-CP provided oxygen and carbon monoxide readings; a Carbon Dioxide Monitor measured carbon dioxide before and after tests. The report describes comparison with ISS Major Constituents Analyzer oxygen readings. Limits: Small samples and a specific duct do not establish whole-cabin behavior. Measurements and sensors are not interchangeable across tests. Source: BASS-II Summary Report, apparatus and test matrices.

outside: No test record in this atlas burned at lunar gravity. Short partial-gravity tests exist as reported findings, not test rows.
MicroFire Atlas reports NASA evidence; these records do not establish mission safety, fire probability, predictions or isolated causal proof.
Investigation overviews describe objectives and scope only. They are not measured test results or detector-performance data.

Summarize only BASS / BASS-II. Retrieved items are a bounded subset, not the entire investigation. BASS and BASS-II are grouped for discovery. The sensor description above is specifically supported by the BASS-II report; it is not a universal specification for all BASS campaigns.
response.summary: At airflow speeds less than 1 cm/s, flames tended to become dim blue and very stable, burning for a long time. Flames survived at airflow less than 1 cm/s.

claims.text: At airflow speeds less than 1 cm/s, flames tended to become dim blue and very stable, burning for a long time.
Flames survived at airflow less than 1 cm/s.
At 5 cm/s airflow, flames spread more slowly and burned longer than at 10 cm/s.
Quenching speeds were between 1 and 5 cm/s, with higher speeds in lower oxygen atmospheres.
